Name: William H. Crogman
Summary: Born in Sint Maarten, Crogman became a classicist, educator and the 11th president of Clark College.
Milestone 1: 1876: Graduates in Atlanta University's first class
Milestone 2: 1895: Helps organize the Negro exhibit at Atlanta's Cotton States Exposition
Milestone 3: 1903–1910: Serves as president of Clark College
Sources: Wikipedia (William H. Crogman)

Name: Alonzo Herndon
Summary: A barber turned businessman, Herndon built Atlanta Life Insurance Company out of a struggling mutual aid society.
Milestone 1: 1883: Arrives in Atlanta and buys a half-interest in a barbershop
Milestone 2: 1905: Buys a struggling mutual aid association and incorporates it
Milestone 3: 1905: Attends the organizing meeting of the Niagara Movement with his son Norris
Milestone 4: 1922: Reorganizes it as Atlanta Life Insurance Company, with assets over $400,000
Connected through: Atlanta Life Insurance; the Niagara Movement
Sources: New Georgia Encyclopedia; Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 210

Name: Ludie Clay Andrews
Summary: Known as the “Dean of Black Nurses,” Andrews won the right for Black nurses to register in Georgia.
Milestone 1: 1914: Founds Grady Hospital's Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses
Milestone 2: 1920: Becomes Georgia's first Black registered nurse after a decade-long fight
Milestone 3: 1928–1948: Superintendent of the Morehouse-Spelman-Atlanta University infirmary
Sources: Georgia Women of Achievement; Wikipedia (Ludie Clay Andrews)

Name: John Wesley Dobbs
Summary: Grand Master of Georgia's Prince Hall Masons, Dobbs led voter registration drives that reshaped Atlanta politics.
Milestone 1: 1932: Elected Grand Master of the Prince Hall Masons
Milestone 2: 1936: Founds the Atlanta Civic and Political League; about 20,000 Black Atlantans register over the next decade
Milestone 3: 1946: Co-founds the Atlanta Negro Voters League with A. T. Walden
Connected through: the Atlanta Negro Voters League; family (Dobbs)
Sources: Wikipedia (John Wesley Dobbs)

Name: Benjamin E. Mays
Summary: President of Morehouse College for 27 years, where his students included Martin Luther King Jr.
Milestone 1: 1940–1967: President of Morehouse College; enrollment grows from 238 to about 1,000
Milestone 2: 1963: Gives the benediction at the March on Washington
Milestone 3: 1968: Delivers the eulogy at Dr. King's funeral
Milestone 4: 1969–1978: On the Atlanta Board of Education during peaceful desegregation
Sources: Wikipedia (Benjamin Mays)

Name: Horace Mann Bond
Summary: An educator and college president whose research supported the case against school segregation.
Milestone 1: 1939–1945: Founding president of Fort Valley State College
Milestone 2: 1945–1957: First African American president of Lincoln University
Milestone 3: 1953: Research supporting the NAACP's Brown v. Board of Education case
Milestone 4: 1957–1971: Dean, then research bureau director, at Atlanta University
Sources: Wikipedia (Horace Mann Bond)

Name: Grace Towns Hamilton
Summary: The first African American woman elected to the Georgia General Assembly, after two decades leading the Atlanta Urban League.
Milestone 1: 1943: Becomes executive director of the Atlanta Urban League
Milestone 2: 1952: Instrumental in opening Grady's Hughes Spalding Pavilion for Black patients and physicians
Milestone 3: 1966: Sworn in to the Georgia General Assembly
Milestone 4: 1973: A principal architect of Atlanta's new City Charter
Sources: Georgia Women of Achievement; Atlanta History Center

Name: Annie L. McPheeters
Summary: A librarian who built Atlanta's Black history collections and helped desegregate its public libraries.
Milestone 1: 1934: Launches the Negro History Collection at the Auburn Branch library
Milestone 2: 1959: Works with advocates to desegregate the Atlanta Public Library
Milestone 3: 1966: First African American reference librarian at Georgia State College
Milestone 4: 1993: A branch library is named in her honor
Sources: New Georgia Encyclopedia

Name: Dr. Asa G. Yancey Sr.
Summary: The first African American physician on staff at Grady, he established the first accredited surgical residency for African Americans in Georgia and Alabama.
Milestone 1: 1948–1958: Chief of surgery at the Tuskegee VA hospital
Milestone 2: 1958: Medical director of Grady's Hughes Spalding Pavilion
Milestone 3: 1964: First African American member of Emory's medical faculty
Milestone 4: 1972: Named medical director of Grady Memorial Hospital
Sources: Wikipedia (Asa G. Yancey Sr.); Find a Grave biography

Name: John Lewis
Summary: A leader of the student civil rights movement who served 17 terms in Congress. He was laid to rest at South-View in 2020.
Milestone 1: 1963–1966: Chairs the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee
Milestone 2: 1965: Attacked by state troopers on “Bloody Sunday” in Selma
Milestone 3: 1987: Begins 17 terms representing Georgia's 5th district
Sources: Wikipedia (John Lewis)

Name: Martin Luther King Sr.
Summary: Pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church for 44 years and an early voting-rights organizer, he was the father of Martin Luther King Jr.
Milestone 1: 1931–1975: Leads Ebenezer Baptist Church after his father-in-law, A. D. Williams
Milestone 2: 1936: Leads a voting-rights march on Atlanta City Hall
Milestone 3: Pushes for equal pay for Black teachers and serves on the Morehouse and Atlanta University boards
Connected through: Ebenezer Baptist Church; the Atlanta NAACP
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 220; Find a Grave (birth year)

Name: A. D. King
Summary: Martin Luther King Jr.'s younger brother, he led protests in Alabama and Kentucky and later co-pastored Ebenezer with his father.
Milestone 1: 1963: His home in Ensley, Alabama, is bombed during the Birmingham campaign
Milestone 2: Leads Louisville demonstrations that help win an open-housing law in Kentucky
Milestone 3: 1968: Becomes co-pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church after his brother's death
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 219; FamilySearch (birth year)

Name: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson
Summary: Raised in Atlanta's Summerhill neighborhood, she became the first and only woman to serve as executive secretary of SNCC.
Milestone 1: 1961: Serves 30 days in jail after a “jail, no bail” protest in South Carolina, then joins the Freedom Rides
Milestone 2: 1966: Becomes executive secretary of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee
Milestone 3: 1967: Dies at 25; her epitaph reads “If you think free, you are free.”
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 238; BlackPast (birth year)

Name: Adam Daniel Williams
Summary: As pastor, Williams grew Ebenezer Baptist Church from a handful of members into a center of political and community life.
Milestone 1: 1917: Helps organize the Atlanta branch of the NAACP, later serving as its president
Milestone 2: Serves as president of the Atlanta Baptist Ministers' Union
Milestone 3: Grandfather of Martin Luther King Jr.
Connected through: Ebenezer Baptist Church; the Atlanta NAACP
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 253; Find a Grave (birth year)

Name: Samuel Woodrow Williams
Summary: A Morehouse philosophy professor and pastor of Friendship Baptist Church who led the Atlanta NAACP.
Milestone 1: 1954–1970: Pastor of Friendship Baptist Church
Milestone 2: 1959: A plaintiff in the successful lawsuit to desegregate Atlanta's city buses
Milestone 3: Chairs Morehouse's philosophy and religion department and holds SCLC leadership roles
Connected through: the Atlanta NAACP; Morehouse College; the SCLC
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 254; Encyclopedia of Arkansas (birth year)

Name: Harold I. Bearden
Summary: Pastor of Big Bethel AME Church, Bearden used weekly radio broadcasts to preach against segregation.
Milestone 1: 1950s–1960s: Pastor of Big Bethel AME Church; president of the Atlanta NAACP
Milestone 2: 1964: Elected the 83rd bishop of the AME Church
Milestone 3: Chairs the Morris Brown College trustees and helps the school win accreditation
Connected through: the Atlanta NAACP; Morris Brown College
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 173; Civil Rights Digital Library (birth year)

Name: Fred C. Bennette Jr.
Summary: One of Dr. King's most trusted aides, Bennette organized sit-ins, voter drives and the SCLC's Operation Breadbasket.
Milestone 1: 1960: As a Morris Brown student, leads the sit-in campaign at Rich's department store
Milestone 2: 1964–1967: First director of SCLC's Operation Breadbasket
Milestone 3: Later advises Gov. Jimmy Carter and Mayor Andrew Young
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 174; Auburn Avenue Research Library finding aid (birth year)

Name: Samuel H. Archer
Summary: Over 33 years at Morehouse, Archer taught math, coached football, served as dean and became the college's fifth president.
Milestone 1: 1905: Joins Morehouse, where he also coaches football to five conference titles
Milestone 2: 1931–1938: President of Morehouse College
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 171

Name: J. W. E. Bowen
Summary: Born enslaved, Bowen became the first African American to earn a PhD at Boston University and later led Gammon Theological Seminary.
Milestone 1: 1887: Earns his PhD at Boston University
Milestone 2: 1893: Becomes Gammon's first full-time African American professor
Milestone 3: 1904: Co-founds the national magazine The Voice of the Negro
Milestone 4: 1906: Opens Gammon as a shelter during the Atlanta race riot
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 179

Name: James P. Brawley
Summary: Brawley served Clark College for 60 years and moved it to the Atlanta University Center.
Milestone 1: 1926–1941: Dean of Clark College
Milestone 2: 1941: Coordinates Clark's move from east Atlanta to the Atlanta University Center
Milestone 3: 1941–1965: President of Clark College
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 181

Name: Alice Dugged Cary
Summary: An educator and librarian who was Atlanta's first Black woman principal and the first librarian of the Auburn Avenue branch.
Milestone 1: 1886: Named principal of the Mitchell Street School
Milestone 2: 1900: Helps open the first free kindergarten for Black children in Atlanta
Milestone 3: 1921: Becomes the first librarian of the Auburn Avenue Branch Library
Connected through: Morris Brown College; the Atlanta Public Library
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 187

Name: Bazoline Usher
Summary: A teacher and principal who became the only African American with an office in Atlanta's City Hall when she was named director of instruction.
Milestone 1: 1943: Organizes Atlanta's first African American Girl Scout troop
Milestone 2: 1951: Named director of instruction for Atlanta's Black schools; opens seven new elementary schools
Milestone 3: 2014: Named a Georgia Woman of Achievement
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 247

Name: Dinah Watts Pace
Summary: Born enslaved, Pace became a teacher and founded one of Georgia's first orphanages for Black children.
Milestone 1: With her brothers, starts a Sunday school that grows into Reed Street Baptist Church
Milestone 2: 1890: Charters the Covington Colored Orphans Home, later the Reed Home and School
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 233

Name: George A. Towns
Summary: One of the first African Americans on the Atlanta University faculty, Towns was a writer, debate coach and voting-rights activist.
Milestone 1: 1905: Takes part in the organizing meeting of the Niagara Movement
Milestone 2: Active in the NAACP and Black voter registration; father of Grace Towns Hamilton
Connected through: the Atlanta NAACP; Atlanta University; the Niagara Movement; family (Towns)
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 245

Name: William A. Fountain
Summary: President of Morris Brown College and later a bishop of the AME Church.
Milestone 1: 1892: Licensed to preach in his hometown of Elberton, Georgia
Milestone 2: 1911–1920: Fifth president of Morris Brown College
Milestone 3: 1920–1952: Bishop in the AME Church
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 200; Prabook (birth year)

Name: Henry McNeal Turner
Summary: A Union Army chaplain, Reconstruction legislator and AME bishop, Turner was one of the most influential Georgians of his era.
Milestone 1: 1863: Becomes the first of 14 African American chaplains in the Union Army
Milestone 2: 1868: Elected to the Georgia legislature, then expelled with the other Black members
Milestone 3: 1880: Becomes the first Southern bishop elected in the AME Church
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), pp. 134–135, 246

Name: Q. V. Williamson
Summary: A real estate broker who became the first African American elected to Atlanta's city government since Reconstruction.
Milestone 1: 1965: Elected to Atlanta's Board of Aldermen (city council)
Milestone 2: Leads the National Association of Real Estate Brokers and works to desegregate housing
Connected through: Morehouse College; the Atlanta Negro Voters League
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 254

Name: John H. Calhoun Jr.
Summary: A civil rights leader and lifelong learner who led the Atlanta NAACP and joined the city council at 74.
Milestone 1: 1956: Serves as president of the Atlanta NAACP
Milestone 2: 1973: Elected to the Atlanta City Council; introduces the resolution creating neighborhood planning units
Connected through: the Atlanta NAACP; Morehouse College; the Atlanta Negro Voters League
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 185

Name: Henry Hugh Proctor
Summary: First Congregational Church's first Black pastor, Proctor turned it into a hub of community services.
Milestone 1: 1894: Begins his ministry at First Congregational Church
Milestone 2: Adds a lending library, kindergarten, job training and an employment bureau
Milestone 3: 1908: Booker T. Washington speaks at the laying of the new church's cornerstone
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 237

Name: Luther Judson Price
Summary: A store owner who became Atlanta's only African American postmaster at the time.
Milestone 1: 1889: Appointed postmaster for South Atlanta, running the post office inside his store
Milestone 2: 1906: Arrested during the race riot on a charge later dismissed
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 236

Name: Irene Dobbs Jackson
Summary: A Spelman French professor who became the first African American to get a card at Atlanta's main public library.
Milestone 1: 1933: Marries Rev. Maynard Jackson in Toulouse, France, where she earns her doctorate
Milestone 2: 1959: Receives a main-branch library card after a lawsuit pushes the library to desegregate
Milestone 3: Mother of Maynard Jackson Jr., Atlanta's first Black mayor
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 216; Wikipedia (Irene Dobbs Jackson)

Name: Cornelius Golightly
Summary: A philosopher and the first African American president of the Detroit School Board, credited with the peaceful desegregation of Detroit's schools. A cenotaph honors him at South-View.
Milestone 1: 1950: Resigns from Olivet College in protest over limits on academic freedom
Milestone 2: First African American on the Milwaukee School Board
Milestone 3: 1969: Becomes dean at Wayne State University
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 203; BlackPast (birth year)

Name: T. M. Alexander
Summary: Founder of one of the nation's most successful Black-owned insurance agencies, Alexander used his business to support the civil rights movement.
Milestone 1: 1955–1956: Insures the cars used in the Montgomery bus boycott after white companies refuse
Milestone 2: 1964: Appointed by President Johnson to help carry out the Civil Rights Act
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 170

Name: Jesse Hill
Summary: President of Atlanta Life Insurance and the first African American president of the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce.
Milestone 1: 1960: Helps launch the Atlanta Inquirer as a voice against discrimination
Milestone 2: 1973–1992: President of Atlanta Life Insurance Company
Milestone 3: First African American to chair Georgia's Board of Regents
Connected through: Atlanta Life Insurance; the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 211; Wikipedia (Jesse Hill)

Name: Herman J. Russell
Summary: Russell built a construction company that helped shape Atlanta's skyline and quietly funded the civil rights movement.
Milestone 1: 1946: At 16, buys his first property with $125 he saved
Milestone 2: Pays bail for jailed activists and gives to the SCLC
Milestone 3: Second African American president of the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce
Connected through: the SCLC; the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 239

Name: Norris B. Herndon
Summary: Alonzo Herndon's only son, he grew Atlanta Life into one of the largest Black-owned businesses in the nation.
Milestone 1: 1905: As a child, attends the Niagara Movement's organizing meeting with his father
Milestone 2: 1927: Succeeds his father as president of Atlanta Life Insurance Company
Connected through: Atlanta University; Atlanta Life Insurance; the Niagara Movement
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 210

Name: Geneva Haugabrooks
Summary: A mortuary owner who opened Haugabrooks Funeral Home on Auburn Avenue.
Milestone 1: 1929: Opens Haugabrooks Funeral Home on Auburn Avenue
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), pp. 68, 208

Name: Freddye Henderson
Summary: A fashion expert who co-founded the first accredited African American travel agency in the nation.
Milestone 1: 1950: First African American to earn a master's in fashion merchandising from NYU
Milestone 2: 1954: Her first trip to a European fashion show leads to Henderson Travel Services
Milestone 3: Arranges trips for Dr. King and Andrew Young and charter tours to West Africa
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 208

Name: Jesse B. Blayton
Summary: Georgia's first Black certified public accountant, Blayton also bought the first Black-owned radio station in the U.S.
Milestone 1: 1928: Becomes the first African American CPA in Georgia
Milestone 2: 1949: Buys WERD, the first U.S. radio station owned by African Americans
Milestone 3: 1995: Inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 175

Name: William F. Penn
Summary: A Yale-trained physician who practiced in Atlanta for 25 years and helped organize the Mercy and Fair Haven medical facilities for Black patients.
Milestone 1: President of the Atlanta Medical Society
Milestone 2: Chief of surgical staff at the Tuskegee veterans' hospital for eight years
Milestone 3: 1934: Aviator Hubert Julian drops wreaths from the air over his graveside at South-View
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), pp. 121–122, 234

Name: Moses Amos
Summary: The first African American licensed as a pharmacist in Georgia.
Milestone 1: 1911: Passes the Georgia pharmacy exam and receives his druggist license
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 170

Name: Miles G. Amos
Summary: A pharmacist who took over his uncle Moses Amos's drugstore and was active in Atlanta politics.
Milestone 1: 1928: Takes over the West Side Drug Store, soon renamed Amos' Drugstore
Milestone 2: 1953: Wins a court decision and election to the City Executive Committee
Milestone 3: 1969: Retires from the drugstore
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 170; SNAC (birth year)

Name: Homer E. Nash
Summary: A physician who practiced on Auburn Avenue for decades and cared for the children of the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home.
Milestone 1: 1910: Earns his medical degree at Meharry and opens his office on Auburn Avenue
Milestone 2: 1963: Named physician of the year by the National Medical Association
Milestone 3: 1965: Named physician of the year by the Georgia Medical Association
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An Atlanta City of the Dead (2018), p. 231; WikiTree (birth year)
